question: Early spell-checkers didn't recognise the word 'cooperation' without a hyphen, so they swapped it for a Californian place name, and it slipped into official UN and EU documents. Which town, the home of Apple, was it?
source_excerpt: dozens of Cupertinos to be found in online documents from the UN, EU, NATO, and other international organizations

extra.why_interesting: Players assume autocorrect fails are a smartphone-era joke. In fact a famous one predates smartphones, made it into official international documents, and even gave its name to the whole phenomenon. The Apple clue lets players reason their way to the answer.
extra.verification_notes: The 'Cupertino effect' is well documented: old spell-checkers replaced unhyphenated 'cooperation' with 'Cupertino', and examples appear in UN/EU documents (https://mentalfloss.com/article/32294/cupertino-effect-11-spell-check-errors-made-it-press).

explanation: The old dictionaries only knew 'co-operation' with a hyphen, and 'Cupertino' was the closest match they had. The mistake was so common that it is now called the 'Cupertino effect'.

question: Before touchscreens, phones guessed your words with a predictive text system called T9. Think of the old keypad: what did the '9' stand for?
source_excerpt: T9 stands for Text on 9 keys.

extra.why_interesting: Millions of people used T9 for years without wondering what the name meant. Picturing an old keypad, with letters spread across the keys 2 to 9 plus the 1 key, gives most players a satisfying 'I can work this out' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia states T9 stands for 'Text on 9 keys', so the 9 means nine keys (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T9_(predictive_text)).

explanation: T9 meant 'Text on 9 keys'. You pressed each key once and the phone worked out which word you meant, instead of you tapping 7 four times to get an S.
